patient.name: Bernard Okwuosa
patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral leg weakness and numbness worsening over 4 months, cannot climb stairs
patient.hpi: Bernard Okwuosa is a 62-year-old retired high school principal with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and numbness that has not responded to pregabalin initiated by his primary care physician. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 8 years ago, and his primary care physician attributed his current symptoms to diabetic peripheral neuropathy. However, his neurologist notes several features atypical for diabetic neuropathy: the weakness is prominent and proximal as well as distal, the course has been rapidly progressive over only 4 months rather than the gradual years-long progression of diabetic neuropathy, and his right upper extremity has recently become involved with hand weakness and difficulty opening jars. He reports bilateral foot and calf numbness and tingling beginning 4 months ago, followed within 6 weeks by prominent thigh weakness making stair-climbing difficult. He struggles to rise from low chairs and has fallen twice. He reports new right hand weakness over the past 6 weeks. He denies bowel or bladder involvement. His HbA1c has been 7.2% for the past year on metformin and sitagliptin. He has no history of alcohol use, recent travel, or toxic exposures. He denies weight loss. A prior NCS performed by his primary care physician 3 years ago showed mild axonal changes attributed to diabetes. He is now referred to neurology for progressive weakness not fitting diabetic neuropathy.

output.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no electrographic seizures recorded. Awake background alpha rhythm at 10 Hz bilaterally, symmetric and reactive. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Right peroneal motor velocity 38.2 m/s (L), Right tibial motor velocity 36.8 m/s (L), Right peroneal conduction block 33% amplitude drop (H), Right sural SNAP amplitude 4.2 uV (L). Mixed demyelinating and axonal features with conduction block at a non-compressive site. EMG shows active denervation with polyphasic motor unit potentials in proximal lower extremity musculature.

Markedly elevated CSF protein at 118 mg/dL with normal cell count (2 WBC/uL) — a pattern of albumino-cytologic dissociation. No pleocytosis. No malignant cells on cytology. No oligoclonal bands. Clinical correlation recommended.
All values within normal limits. IgA 284 mg/dL (normal range). Anti-NF155 and anti-CNTN1 negative. No M-spike on repeat SPEP.

findings.description: Cervical spine: Mild C5-C6 neural foraminal narrowing without cord compression or cord signal abnormality. Lumbar spine: Mild L4-L5 and L5-S1 disc bulging without significant canal stenosis. No epidural collection. Nerve roots: Bilateral posterior nerve root enhancement at L4-S1 on gadolinium-enhanced sequences; mildly thickened, clumped cauda equina nerve roots with gadolinium enhancement bilaterally. Conus medullaris: normal signal.

output.impression: 1. Bilateral gadolinium enhancement of posterior nerve roots at L4-S1 with mildly thickened, clumped cauda equina nerve roots — findings consistent with inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathy. 2. Mild C5-C6 neural foraminal narrowing without cord compression. 3. Mild L4-L5 and L5-S1 disc bulging without significant canal stenosis. 4. Normal conus medullaris signal. No epidural abscess. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings: Segmental demyelination and remyelination with onion bulb formations (concentric Schwann cell processes wrapping single axons — hallmark of repeated demyelination)
Moderate endoneurial fibrosis. Patchy mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate (CD8+ T cells and macrophages) in endoneurium and perineurium.
Vasculitis: ABSENT — no epineurial or endoneurial vasculitis.
Congo red: Negative for amyloid. No IgG/IgA/IgM/complement deposits on myelin.
Electron microscopy: Onion bulbs confirmed; widely-spaced myelin lamellae absent (anti-MAG excluded).
output.impression: Sural nerve biopsy shows segmental demyelination and remyelination with onion bulb formations and macrophage-associated demyelination. Patchy endoneurial T-cell and macrophage infiltrate. Moderate axonal loss. No vasculitis. Congo red negative for amyloid. Widely-spaced myelin lamellae absent on electron microscopy. Findings are consistent with a chronic inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.
recommended_actions: Repeat electrophysiology recommended to monitor interval change.

output.query: CIDP superimposed on diabetic neuropathy diagnosis treatment IVIG

results.citation: Laughlin RS et al. (2009) CIDP in diabetes. Neurology 73:697-701.
results.summary: CIDP occurs 11x more frequently in diabetic patients. Distinguishing features from diabetic neuropathy: proximal weakness, rapid progression, CSF protein >80 mg/dL, demyelinating NCS with conduction block. IVIG response rate 70-80% in CIDP with diabetes.

results.citation: Vallat JM et al. (2010) Nerve biopsy in CIDP. J Neurol 257:1386-1389.
results.summary: Onion bulb formations on sural nerve biopsy confirm CIDP when NCS criteria are borderline. Anti-NF155/CNTN1 positive nodopathy variants are IVIG-refractory — test before initiating IVIG.

output.summary: IVIG, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange are established immunomodulatory treatments for CIDP with class I–II evidence. Randomized trials show approximately 70–80% short-term response rate to IVIG in CIDP. CIDP occurs at higher frequency in patients with diabetes mellitus, and electrodiagnostic criteria for CIDP in this population require attention to conduction block at non-compressive sites. IgA measurement before IVIG administration is standard practice. Nodal/paranodal antibody status (anti-NF155, anti-CNTN1) may predict differential treatment response.

output.proposed: IVIG 2g/kg induction + Metformin 1000 mg twice daily + Atorvastatin 40 mg daily + Lisinopril 10 mg daily

interactions.description: IVIG may cause transient glucose fluctuations due to sucrose or glucose stabilizers in some formulations. Monitor blood glucose during and 24-48 hours after IVIG infusion. Use sucrose-free IVIG formulations (Gammagard Liquid, Privigen) in diabetic patients.

warnings: Use sucrose-free IVIG formulation for this diabetic patient. Monitor glucose during infusion.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) superimposed on mild diabetic axonal polyneuropathy
critical_actions: IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days induction (IgA safe); use sucrose-free formulation in diabetic patient
IVIG maintenance 1 g/kg every 3-4 weeks (assess response at 3 months)
Monitor NCS at 6 months to document treatment response
Continue diabetes management; HbA1c optimization reduces axonal component
If IVIG fails at 6 months: consider oral prednisone taper or subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mixed demyelinating-axonal polyneuropathy with conduction block at popliteal segment (non-compressive site) in bilateral peroneal and tibial nerves; velocities 36-38 m/s; proximal EMG involvement
CSF protein 118 mg/dL with WBC 2/uL — albumino-cytologic dissociation confirming CIDP
IgA 284 mg/dL (IVIG safe); anti-NF155 and anti-CNTN1 negative (standard CIDP, not nodopathy)
Bilateral posterior nerve root and cauda equina gadolinium enhancement — hypertrophic nerve roots consistent with CIDP
Segmental demyelination, onion bulb formations, macrophage-associated demyelination; no vasculitis, no amyloid
CIDP occurs 11x more frequently in diabetic patients; IVIG response 70-80%; rapid 4-month progression with UE involvement atypical for diabetic neuropathy alone
Use sucrose-free IVIG in diabetic patient; monitor glucose during infusion; IgA level confirms IVIG safety

differential.key_features: Well-controlled HbA1c 7.2% and only mild NCS 3 years ago cannot explain the severity; rapid 4-month progression, proximal involvement, and upper extremity weakness are NOT features of diabetic neuropathy alone; conduction block at non-compressive sites is diagnostic for CIDP
No family history of neuropathy, no pes cavus, no hammer toes; rapid onset over 4 months (CMT1 is lifelong and slowly progressive); no high-arched feet or distal atrophy in youth
MMN is a purely motor neuropathy without sensory involvement; this patient has prominent sensory loss; MMN does not cause albumino-cytologic dissociation in CSF
No M-spike on SPEP, no papilledema, no organomegaly, no skin changes, normal VEGF — POEMS excluded by absence of mandatory criteria and normal SPEP

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: The anchoring trap is HbA1c 7.2% with prior NCS showing mild axonal changes — clinician must recognize this is insufficient to explain the severity, rapidity, and proximal extent of the current presentation

CONDUCTION BLOCK AT NON-COMPRESSIVE SITE: The 33-35% CMAP amplitude drop at the popliteal segment (not an entrapment site) is the pathognomonic finding for CIDP — must specifically request proximal segment testing
DIABETIC CIDP COMORBIDITY: CIDP occurs 11x more frequently in diabetic patients; the well-controlled HbA1c 7.2% actually argues AGAINST diabetes as the cause of this severe neuropathy
ALBUMINO-CYTOLOGIC DISSOCIATION: CSF protein 118 mg/dL with WBC 2/uL is the cardinal CSF signature of CIDP — must obtain LP in any patient with suspected CIDP

UPPER EXTREMITY INVOLVEMENT: Onset of right hand weakness and decreased grip at 4 months confirms the neuropathy is ascending beyond the expected length-dependent pattern — key atypical feature for DPNP
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute all symptoms to diabetic neuropathy when HbA1c is well-controlled at 7.2% and prior NCS showed only mild changes — the severity and rapidity demand additional diagnosis
Do not give IVIG without first checking IgA level — IVIG is absolutely contraindicated in IgA deficiency (risk of anaphylaxis)
Do not miss the conduction block at popliteal segment — must specifically request proximal segment NCS recordings, not just standard distal recordings

red_herrings.data_point: History of type 2 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 8 years ago, HbA1c 7.2%) with prior NCS showing mild axonal changes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Creates strong anchoring toward 'worsening diabetic neuropathy' as the explanation for current symptoms, potentially leading to premature closure and missed CIDP diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c 7.2%) with only mild prior NCS cannot explain severe mixed demyelinating-axonal neuropathy with proximal involvement and upper extremity weakness developing over 4 months. The pre-existing mild axonal component from diabetes is a red herring — CIDP is the new superimposed disease requiring IVIG.

red_herrings.data_point: Pregabalin failure over 3 months reported by referring physician
red_herrings.intended_effect: May suggest to the clinician that neuropathic symptoms are refractory to treatment, potentially leading to dose escalation rather than seeking an alternative inflammatory diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pregabalin addresses only symptom control and has no effect on the underlying CIDP process. Treatment failure of symptomatic agents is expected in CIDP without disease-modifying immunotherapy (IVIG). This should prompt escalation to diagnosis and immunotherapy, not dose escalation of pain medications.
